title: Human L2/3 pyramidal connections ran mostly downward in two slice cohorts, but depth and cell degrees did not explain the near-absence of cycles in one cohort
abstract: Peng et al. (2024) reported directed and mostly acyclic connectivity among human layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons. We tested whether cortical depth sets connection direction and explains this topology. We used the public Planert tables of the same recordings (898 one-way pairs, 21 donors), Allen Synaptic Physiology human and mouse slices, and MICrONS mouse electron microscopy. In the Planert cohort, 66.4% of one-way connections went from the shallower to the deeper cell (95% donor interval 62.4% to 70.9%; 18 of 21 donors above half). The share increased from 56% at gaps below 50 um to 78% at 100 to 200 um. The independent Allen human cohort gave 61.9% (51.2% to 70.0%, 105 pairs). The depth rule explained only about 20% of the cycle deficit. Only 2 of 146 one-way triangles were cyclic. A random graph gave 35.1, a distance and depth model 28.4, and a null with fixed cell in- and out-degrees 14.5 (95% range 7 to 23). Fixed degrees plus depth and distance weights gave 12.5 to 13.4. Only 3 of 882 one-way edges went against the best order of cells in each cluster. Depth, channel number and cell properties predicted held-out direction in at most 71% of pairs. All three experimenters had fewer cycles than the fixed-degree null. The small Allen human cohort showed no deficit (2 of 7 cyclic, null 1.7), but this test had little power. In intact mouse L2/3, proofread axons did not connect preferentially to deeper cells (ratio 0.71, 0.44 to 1.09), although axon-dendrite proximity was higher toward them. Limitations: curated calls from one laboratory, slice-plane depth, small replication cohorts and one EM mouse. The cause of the missing cycles remains open. The bundle has new code, aggregate results, figures, hashes and a retrieval script; external record-level data are not bundled.

citations.reason: Tests depth as an explanation of the reported directed and acyclic topology; finds the acyclic structure is not explained by depth or degrees, and is not visible in a small independent cohort.
